title: Multiregion Access Decision Attenuator Notes
content:
Context and goal:

This doc captures an exploratory set of ideas for where to place and how to behave the "access decision attenuator" — a small, performance-aware layer that shapes and enforces access policy checks across multi-region routing and the control plane. It originated from the outage postmortem (PLAT-4321) where central PDP contention amplified latency spikes and caused cross-region failovers to degrade service.

Why "attenuator"?
- We want a component that can modulate policy enforcement strictness based on context (latency budget, region isolation, tenant risk level).
- Not a replacement for PDP or PDP caching; more of a tactical enforcement layer that:
  - enforces local, cheap checks (token validity, role claims) at the edge,
  - defers or degrades non-critical attributes to async or weaker enforcement when necessary,
  - emits clear telemetry and fallbacks when attenuation occurs.

Primary constraints we must observe:
- Latency SLOs for serving requests: <= 50ms p95 for routing decision plus auth checks in hosted tiers.
- Regulatory boundaries: data residency (EU-only decisioning for EU tenants), audit retention requirements for enterprise tenants.
- Threat model: nothing in attenuator should allow silent privilege escalation; any degradations must be explicit and auditable.
- Operational simplicity: operators must be able to reason about attenuation state per-region and per-tenant.

Candidate enforcement points and roles
(ordered by proximity to traffic, with tradeoffs):
1) Edge proxy (L7 sidecar / regional ingress):
   - Checks: token signature, token audience, token expiry, cheap claim checks (tenant id present, scope list), small denylist checks.
   - Pros: lowest latency, preserves region boundaries, cheap to scale.
   - Cons: limited attribute context (no user attributes outside token), limited ability to evaluate complex ABAC rules.
2) Edge-attached attunuator service (lightweight, co-located with ingress):
   - Checks: expand token via introspect to include role, tenant risk score; quick ABAC decisions based on claims cached locally.
   - Pros: more expressivity while staying local; can implement attenuation policies (e.g., allow read-only fallback)
   - Cons: cache staleness, complexity of local caches invalidation across regions.
3) Regional PDP cache + policy layer (in-region but central):
   - Checks: authoritative PDP decisions for region-scoped policies (data residency, tenant agreements).
   - Pros: consistent within region, supports more attributes.
   - Cons: higher latency than edge; needs autoscaling per-region.
4) Global control-plane PDP (centralized, slow path):
   - Checks: wide-scope policies (global role mappings, org-level overrides, feature gates tied to billing/contract).
   - Pros: single source of truth, easier policy authoring.
   - Cons: high latency, single-point if used synchronously.

Attenuation strategies (how the attenuator degrades enforcement when budget constrained):
- Mode 1: Strict (normal ops) — edge denies on token failures, requires PDP allow for sensitive operations.
- Mode 2: Conservative relax (mild overload) — edge allows requests that pass token sanity checks but marks them for post-hoc audit; sensitive ops still require synchronous PDP.
- Mode 3: Read-only fallback (region outage) — write/modify requests are rejected/local-queued; reads allowed if token + tenant claims match, with sampled logging.
- Mode 4: Emergency bypass (extreme global outage) — only for emergency support/shift; requires org-level override and creates immediate incident.

Policy decision caching and TTL heuristics:
- Cache keys: (tenant, principal-id, role-set-hash, resource-pattern, action, region, policy-version).
- TTL by risk tier: low-risk TTL 120s, medium 30s, high-risk 5s (high-risk includes admin/scoped write ops).
- Explicit invalidation hooks: policy rollouts bump policy-version; token revocations emit hash-invalidation to region caches via pubsub.

Observability & Auditability requirements:
- Every attenuation event must record: request-id, tenant, principal, region, attenuation-mode, reason code, PDP decision-id if present.
- Sampling: 100% for writes affected by attenuation; 1% for reads with attenuation, with ability to increase sampling on suspicious patterns.
- Dashboards: per-region attenuator health, attenuation-rate (by tenant), mean added latency, cache hit ratio.

Decision model: ABAC + RBAC blend
- Base model: RBAC for coarse-grained roles (billing-admin, devops, service-account), ABAC for contextual gates (time-of-day, region-affinity, recent MFA).
- Evaluation flow:
  1) Edge verifies token and role claims. If role claim maps to low-risk and resource is read-only, short-circuit allow.
  2) If action is sensitive, consult local cache ABAC policy. If cache miss, call regional PDP with request fingerprint.
  3) If regional PDP unavailable and policy is non-blocking by tenant policy, switch to conservative relax + audit.

Open questions / risks to address:
- How do we make attenuation decisions transparent to product teams? (proposal: expose per-tenant attenuation_config and incident timeline in Console)
- Key rotation + token revocation propagation. Pubsub invalidations may be delayed; do we hold short TTLs for revoke-sensitive claims?
- Cross-region trust: should one region accept a cached claim minted in another region? (recommend: only if signed with global KMS and tenant-config allows cross-region tokens)
- Complexity vs. safety: the more modes we support, the higher cognitive load for operators. Keep modes minimal and well-documented.

Implementation sketch (phases)
- Phase 0: Observability-only deploy: collect authz decision latencies, cache hits, PDP error rates per-region. (2 weeks)
- Phase 1: Edge token hardening + basic attenuation flags: reject obviously malformed tokens, allow conservative relax for non-sensitive ops; implement dashboards. (4 weeks)
- Phase 2: Local attunuator service with cache + policy-versioning; introduce TTL tiers and invalidation pubsub. Start per-tenant attenuation config. (8 weeks)
- Phase 3: Policy rollout tooling + Console exposure + canary attenuation toggles (A/B). (6 weeks)

Operational playbook snippets
- If regional PDP error rate > 5% and attenuation rate > 1% for more than 5m: escalate to platform on-call, enable read-only fallback for impacted region(s).
- If we detect elevated post-hoc denial audits from attenuated allow paths: revert relaxation for affected tenant(s) and notify customer success.

Notes / references
- See PLAT-4321 for outage timeline that motivated this design.
- Proposed SDK additions: client headers to declare latency budget and a boolean "allow-attenuation" to surface intent.
- Security review items: ensure the attenuator cannot be used to escalate privileges via claim substitution; require token proof-of-possession for any mutation path when attenuation is in effect.

Next steps (for this doc):
- Technical spike: prototype edge-attached attunuator with a Redis local cache and PDP stub to simulate 95th percentile latencies. (owner: Daniel Reed)
- Security review: schedule threat model pass with security (owner: Marta López)
- Product consult: define which product operations can tolerate Conservative Relax vs Read-only fallback (owner: Jin Park)

Unresolved todo lines (notes to self):
- draw sequence diagram for token issuance -> edge check -> regional PDP -> global PDP fallback (TODO: ascii seq diag)
- validate policy-version bump semantics with release-engineering
- finalize sample audit schema (fields + retention)

End of notes.
